cells.tense: The ending has already been made, and the practice is being kept without a wake.
cells.ask: Set one thing you hold to aside from the practice this week. Keep your hours at the rest. Let what's left standing settle it.
cells.core:
You can end things and stay at your work. The practice keeps its hours while something beside it gets set down — no announcement, it's simply done, and you're still there at the time you said you would be. That's harder than the ending itself, and it's what the hours were built to hold. The clearing comes from what you notice, not from a rule about when to quit: something is finished, and you stop because it's finished.

Endings like this don't cost you the thing you've built; they give it room. What holds is that the hours keep their shape whether or not the ending was the right one — you'll know inside a few days how it settled, and that answer is yours. Set the thing down, keep the practice running, and let the two of them sit beside each other for the next stretch of days.
cells.sheetLine: You can end something without wrecking what you've built.

cells.tense: You are standing in a future where the thing has failed, and you end it before that future can arrive.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're about to cut. Carry it two more weeks before you touch it. If it's still wrong then, end it properly.
cells.core:
You keep clearing ground ahead of yourself, and the ground doesn't get planted. Something starts, and before it can be bad or good, it's over — the ending gets done first so the test isn't needed. That's a flinch with a plan.

What you're trying to build only grows in the space between starting and stopping. Each early end resets that clock. You don't need another ending. You need one thing to survive long enough to disappoint you. Let the two weeks pass and see what's there — some of it will be worth keeping, and the part that isn't can still be ended later, when it's actually finished.

cells.tense: You are still keeping an old practice alive because stopping it reads to you as quitting, not clearing.
cells.ask: Say out loud what one habit in your routine is still for. Then take the next week off it and watch what you reach for instead.
cells.core:
You're maintaining something that's already finished. The routine runs, the hours get given, and nothing in it moves you anymore — yet stopping reads as quitting on the person who started it. So it stays, and it costs you the aliveness the practice was built to hold.

Keeping a promise and keeping a habit look the same from the outside. The tell is whether the thing still feeds you or only the idea of you. Whatever's over there was true once, and setting it down doesn't erase that. Pick the one to test, and let the week of not doing it tell you what the habit was actually holding.

cells.tense: Something in the routine has already ended, and you are still calling it a rough patch.
cells.ask: Write down the one piece of the routine you'd defend if asked. Notice what your hand does with the ones you can't. Keep the first, stop forcing the rest for now.
cells.core:
Part of what you do has gone quiet, and you've absorbed the quiet as normal. The hours still get given, the shape of the week is unchanged, and one piece inside it stopped asking anything of you. What you'd call a slow stretch is an old form finishing while the new one waits, small, in the same routine, not yet the thing you protect.

Naming what's over is what lets the rest be chosen instead of carried. You don't have to decide the whole routine tonight. Decide one piece, and let your defense of it show you which of the others you're only keeping out of habit.
